                                    I.      INTRODUCTION

       Nancy Frazier Thompson, Nancy Frazier Thompson Trust, Linnabery Family Trust,

Rexford Grant Keele, Geral Greer, Harrison's Majestic Oaks Cattle Ranch Renewal LLC, Gordon

A and Sheryl L Brown, Wayne and Mary Brown, Gary Brian Robinson, Walker Barton Harkins,

DCA San Gabriel Ranch LLC, Jeffrey Frank Kindschuh and Bell Hudson, RFHDAH LP, Rowena

Guess, Manena Rueffer, Bertram Ranch, LLC, Robert and Bette Jordan Trust, Jack Hornsby, Jr.,

David L and Monya K Giles, Alexander D and Lindsey C Hamilton, ATXA Syndicates LLC, Judith

Elizabeth Beauford, Gibson Lewis, Erin L. Rowe and Kelly S. Rowe, John Alvin Bird and Laura

Ann Bird, McCormick Children's Family LP, Maude Allen, John M. Wyatt, Jr., 99 Gold Star

Holdings 2 LLC, Dr. John McCormick, Jr. and Kathy Jo McCormick, Naveen Kumar Asuthker

and Aarthi Doulagar, Dayaker Thumma and Victoria Rani Thumma, Robert B. Insall, Joshua David

and Katelyn Ashley Fiechtner, and Alton Corder Bishop and Shirlene Bishop (collectively referred

to as “G4 Opposition Alliance”), and J Barto Arnold III and Sherrie Arnold (the “Arnolds”), (the

G4 Opposition Alliance and the Arnolds hereinafter collectively referred to as “Underwood

Parties”) timely file this Initial Post-Hearing Brief opposing Segments G41, G42, G43, G44, G45

and F8 and supporting Route 894, the Best Meets Route, under SOAH Order No. 6.

                            II.     SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

       After 5 days of hearing, there was not a single expert, party or landowner that advocated

for any routes utilizing Segments G41, G42, G43, G44, G45 or F8 (“G4 Opposition Segments”),

nor were those segments even mentioned in any cross-examination. They weren’t included in any

of the focus routes. Furthermore, these 6 segments were included in only 17 of the 122 routes (only

13.93%) that were selected and submitted by Casey Petty, PE, PMP to be filed with the CCN



                                                                                      Page 3 of 19
 Application.1 The reason is clear. Routes including these segments underperform in most of the

PURA factor categories listed on the Environmental Assessment.2 At a minimum, they are more

expensive, longer, affect more habitable structures, cross more than double the amount of cultural

resources sites, and come within 1,000 feet of cultural resource sites more than three times than

that of Route 894.3 Staying within at least 500 feet of the centerline, Segment G44 parallels the

Russell Fork of the San Gabriel River (“San Gabriel”) its entire length and crosses the San Gabriel

numerous times, impetuously fracturing tracts of generational land. Deciding on a route that

includes any of the G4 Opposition Segments makes zero sense and would go against what is

required under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). Making the decision on what

route to choose isn’t the hard part, it is living with that choice.

                                              III.   ARGUMENT

            The Underwood Parties are a group of neighbors with property along the G4 Opposition

Segments. They oppose all routes that include the G4 Opposition Segments because of the

significant negative environmental impact and harm to community values in the area, including

the cost, habitable structure count, and the effect on generational land. The ALJs and Commission

should select Route 894 or any other route that avoids the southernmost portion of the study area

and the San Gabriel to avoid these concerns that should be fatal to selection of any route through

that area.

A.          APPLICATION AND ROUTE ADEQUACY (ISSUE NO. 1)

            The Application is sufficient.

C.          PUBLIC INPUT (ISSUE NO. 4)

            Public input was sufficient and identified concerns with proximity to residences and
            subsequent effect on aesthetics, land use, health and wildlife.

            Joint Applicants hosted three public meetings and developed a website to solicit comments,

concerns and input from residents, landowners, public oﬃcials, and interested parties. 4 In total,

825 people attended the public meetings, and Joint Applicants received 81 responses via

questionnaires.5 The questionnaire provided on the website and public meetings asked for input

regarding land use, paralleling, and community values/resources, and asked Respondents to rank

various factors by importance.6

            In the Application, Joint Applicants state that respondents “consistently expressed the base

concern regarding the proximity of any proposed route to their residence and the subsequent effect

they believed the project may have on aesthetics, land use or land value, health and/or wildlife.”7

E.        ROUTE (ISSUE NOS. 8-10)

                  Weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC

                  a.       Statutory Criteria

                           i.     Community values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)




8
    Oncor & LCRA TSC, Exh. 1 at 208.


                                                                                 Page 6 of 19
             Neither statute nor the Commission’s rules formally define “community values.” While

Joint Applicants also do not define community values; they do provide examples that should be

considered in light of community values such as habitable structures within 500 feet of the

centerline of the transmission line, irrigated pasture or croplands and comments received from

members of the public.9 Joint Applicants also discuss community resources simultaneously with

community values. Kimley-Horn and Halff defines “community resources” as “an area or other

natural or human resource recognized by a national, regional, or local community.” They provide

examples such as parks, recreational areas, historical and archeological sites or scenic vistas.10 The

Underwood Parties represent a community of 36 landowners that have come together in force to

represent the area surrounding the G4 Opposition Segments. They are a community of landowners

who are noted in the EA as responding in a regional capacity independent of and in supplement to

questionnaires provided at the public participation meetings. They came together early and

submitted narratives, as shown above, to express their concerns related to the G4 Opposition

Segments11, not only in regard to their own property and well-being, but to that of the overall

heritage and legacy of their properties in light of archaeological resources and to those

environmental concerns surrounding the San Gabriel and the Golden-Cheeked Warbler (“GCW”)

as shown throughout their testimonies and the testimony of Jennifer Blair.

            Robert Insall’s property has been in his family since 1941.12 His property includes four

contiguous tracts of land that run from north to south. If placed on his property, the transmission

 line would dissect every single tract, causing fragmentation in the most egregious way.13 Not only

would this be detrimental to his farming practices and vineyard operations, but it would be

devastating to the GCW habitats he has sited on his property.14 Likewise, the transmission line

would dissect Mr. Harkins property in half, coming within 500-700 feet of his home.15 The line

would also dissect the Bertram Ranch’s 189 acre ranch, while adding a turning structure and

destroying their hay fields that are used for cattle operations. The line would threaten the potential

archeological sites on their property evidenced by the Native American artifacts they have found.16

On Wayne and Mary Brown’s property, the transmission line would parallel the San Gabriel,

almost directly next to its bank, over excellent soil underneath their hay field, through the Trinity

Aquifer recharge area, and a pioneer settlement. It would eliminate several hardwood trees that are

incredibly old. The final San Gabriel crossing on their property would run the line over their front

gate.17 Other Underwood Parties continue to face similar concerns such as Erin and Kelly Rowe,

who would have the line located 300-400 feet from their home.18 This property has been in their

family for 4 generations, and they would have to cross beneath the transmission line every day

coming and going from their residence.19 Jeff Kindschuh and Bell Hudson own approximately 60

acres that was part of the Carson Ranch. The original Carson Ranch home, built in approximately

1892, was fully restored in 2019 and is used as a guest house.20 Additionally, Mr. Kindschuh and

perennial creeks that lead to the San Gabriel. All their land is currently under wildlife management

and home to the GCW, Blue Heron, turkey and other wildlife. The transmission line would pose a

significant threat to those habitats.21

            Mr. Harrison testified on behalf of the Majestic Oaks Cattle Ranch that their land has been

in their family for over 100 years. It contains approximately 98 acres of beautiful views alongside

the San Gabriel and throughout its Heritage Oak and Heritage Pecan groves, which support

environmental and wildlife systems. The transmission line would fragment their property on their

central to eastern side and close to the San Gabriel, eventually crossing the San Gabriel at the

southern edge of their tract.22 These stories continue through the remaining testimonies that were

filed on behalf of each landowner in the G4 Opposition Alliance. These aren’t properties recently

purchased in the flat plains with no vegetation and little environmental concern. The area of the

G4 Opposition Segments is a community resource – as it is made up of a small community of

landowners across a regional area that are concerned about the environmental impact to that of the

GCW, the San Gabriel River and their family legacies contained within each tract of land.

                            ii.      Recreational and Park Areas; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B)

            Not Addressed.

                            iii.     Aesthetic and Historical Values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C)

            There are no formal guidelines for managing visual resources. Aesthetic impacts occur

when the ROW, lines or structures of a transmission line system alter the character of the existing

visual environment. The significance of the impact is directly related to the quality of the view in



21
     Id. at 4-5.
22
     Underwood Parties, Exh.10 at 3-5.


                                                                                          Page 9 of 19
 the case of natural scenic areas or the importance of the existing setting in the use and enjoyment

of an area in valued community resources and recreational areas.23 It is impossible to eliminate the

visual impacts of a new transmission line, so the focus should be on identifying the least intrusive

option when taking into account the community values previously discussed.

           Routes using the G4 Opposition Segments not only parallel the San Gabriel for most of its

30–35-mile length, but they also cross the San Gabriel in numerous places. Most, if not all, of the

homes along G44 and G45 either have the San Gabriel running through their property or they are

adjacent to it. The San Gabriel provides support for vegetation, wildlife and beautiful views of the

river itself, along the with groves of trees it supports. While other alternative segments, including

those on Route 894 have pretty views, none is crisscrossed like the G4 Opposition Segments do

the San Gabriel. Choosing to put a 765-kV transmission line almost on top of the San Gabriel goes

directly against protecting aesthetic values in finding the least intrusive and destructive route.

                            iv.    Environmental Integrity; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D)

           Several intervenors have cited environmental concerns regarding the location of the

transmission line. The Underwood Parties also strive to maintain the integrity of and manage the

land to enhance the wildlife population by fighting to keep the transmission line off the G4

Opposition Segments. Jennifer Blair, a Certified Wildlife Biologist and owner of Blair Wildlife

Consulting, LLC, testified on behalf of the Underwood Parties, specifically with regard to the

GCW.24 Ms. Blair has studied the area surrounding the G4 Opposition Segments as well as she has

conducted numerous site studies within and around Burnet County, which includes extensive work

on a property used as a mitigation bank that extends from the northern shores of Lake Buchanan

     Oncor & LCRA TSC, Exh. 1 at 247.
24
     Underwood Parties, Exh. 34.


                                                                                       Page 10 of 19
 to an area just north of Segment J31, to identify and document suitable habitats for the GCW.25 In

discussing the purpose of mitigation banks, Ms. Blair stated they exist to counter the negative

impact to GCW habitat throughout its range and lack of other available regional conservation

solutions.26 While Mr. Marusak testified that modifications were made to the mitigation bank

located along J31 as shown in Appendix C to the Application27; they are at best just on the edge of

the mitigation bank. It appears the transmission line ROW would extend into the mitigation bank,

destroying some of the GCW habitat. Ms. Blair details that GCW has site fidelity, which means

that they return repeatedly to the area where it was born to breed.28 She states, “Destroying that

particular habitat prevents the Warbler from returning and breeding….Even when the Warbler

relocates slightly, the loss of habitat extends beyond just the actual trees and growth that are

cleared…Clearing 200 feet of habitat actually results in more habitat loss.          Research has

demonstrated these significant edge effects push the Warbler even further than just the

construction.”29 Whether J31 crosses the mitigation bank or not, it is clear from its proximity that

the edge effects will impact the habitat specifically set aside for the GCW’s protection. This would

be devastating to the GCW given its already dwindling habitat.

            Additionally, Ms. Blair also states habitat required for the GCW is comprised of mature

oak and juniper woodlands, particularly along riverbeds and riparian drainages.30 While her study

has few confirmed sitings on the G4 Opposition Segments, Ms. Blair confidently stated, “The

GCW is absolutely present in other areas in the study area…Basically anywhere you find mature

critical habitat, and help maintain the natural processes that sustain both aquatic and terrestrial

ecosystems.”32 Protection of these riparian areas is not only crucial to the GCW, but also to the

overall environmental health of the area.

                    b.       Commission Rule Criteria

                             ii.   Costs; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

            Cost is always an important factor to consider in evaluating these routes. Ultimately, the

costs are passed down to the rate payers and thus it is imperative we choose a less expensive route

that can also balance the other PURA factors. The cheapest route amongst the alternative routes is

Route 469 at $1,636,232,000 and the most expensive route is Route 910 at $1,857,768,000. 33

Although Route 469 is the cheapest route, it does not balance the PURA factors well in other

However, Route 894’s cost is $1,680,919,000, which is less than 3% difference. It is cheaper than

Route Cherokee G, Route 392 and Route 296. However, it is slightly more expensive than Staff’s

Route 487. The aforementioned routes are cheaper than any route including the G4 Opposition

Segments, which range from $1,724,702,000 to $1,857,768,000.34

                              iii.   Moderation of Impact on the Affected Community and
                                     Landowners; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

           Not addressed.

                              iv.    Paralleling; 16 TAC 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iii) Criteria

           Parallelling is often heavily discussed within these CCN cases. While it didn’t take center

stage in this proceeding, it was discussed and is an important factor to consider in preventing

fragmentation of more land. Ms. Petty outlines in her memorandum that Route 894 parallels

existing compatible rights-of-way for approximately 43.9% of its length.35 While it isn’t the route

with the highest percentage of parallels, it comes close to PUC Staff’s recommended Route 487 at

49.64%, Cherokee G at 46.68%, and Wulf Bluff’s recommended Route 392 at 38.62%. The route

with the highest paralleling is Route 1164.36

                              v.     Prudent Avoidance; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv)

           The Commission defines prudent avoidance as “[t]he limiting of exposures to electric and

magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.”37 Prudent

avoidance also considers what can be done in different settings, such as rural versus urban areas,

 where routing options and the opportunities to make routing changes differ. This does not mean a

proposed transmission line must avoid habitable structures at all costs, but reasonable alternatives

must be considered.38 Maximizing distance from residences was the highest priority for

respondents to Joint Applicants’ open-house questionnaires.39

           Routes including the G4 Opposition Segments range from having 120-157 habitable

structures affected. Segment G41 alone has 25 habitable structures. Ms. Perkins testified on cross-

examination that “the number of habitable structures is an indicator…which is directly tied into

prudent avoidance.”40 Additionally, Mr. Poole agreed with the statement that “additional expense

and implication of mitigation measures should result in affecting fewer habitable structures, not

more habitable structures.”41 While each of the routes in this case arguably satisfies prudent

avoidance, Route 894 leads the way as it affects only 85 habitable structures, which is only 5 more

than the routes with the fewest habitable structures.

           Not Addressed.

                     d.       Best Route Alternative

           There have been several routes offered throughout this case that have offered solutions to

one problem or another and balancing one PURA factor over another. However, the route that

should be picked should be one that best balances the factors identified in PURA. It may be argued

that the EA doesn’t always paint the full picture of the properties, environmental issues and

ignored. Route 894 is arguably the best route based on the factors provided in PURA as shown

structures, has fewer stream and cultural resource crossings.42 Route 894 also avoids the more

notable and clearly identifiable areas of GCW habitat, thereby fulling the requirement to avoid

environmentally sensitive areas.

H.          TPWD’S RECOMMENDATION AND COMMENTS (ISSUE NO. 16)

                    Did the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department provide any recommendations
                    or informational comments regarding this application in accordance with
                    section 12.0011(b) of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Code? If so, how should the
                    Commission respond through its order?

            TPWD responded to Joint Applicant’s request for information concerning environmental

and land use constraints or other issues within the study area.43 Ms. Julie Jones is clear in TPWD’s

recommendation that new transmission lines be routed along “existing roads, pipelines,

transmission lines, or other utility ROW and easements to reduce habitat fragmentation.”44

Additionally, TPWD recommends avoiding routing any transmission lines through GCW habitat,

and only if it is not avoidable do they have recommendations on how to mitigate.45 The image in

Ms. Blair’s testimony is clear that there is GCW habitat located through J31 and also through the

G4 Opposition Segments.46 Dr. Morrison, testifying on behalf of the Colorado River Alliance and

                                                VI.   CONCLUSION

           Mr. Marusak stated in cross-examination on June 8 that the environmental consultant’s

“mantra” is to “avoid, minimize, and mitigate.”48 Link N3 Opposition Landowners’ admitted

Exhibit 12 shows the top 30 routes and of those “Top 30” routes, not a single route includes any

of the G4 Opposition Segments.49 Routes including any G4 Opposition Segments are more

expensive, longer, have considerably more habitable structures and threaten approximately 20

miles of the San Gabriel River along Segment G44. The Underwood Partis urge the ALJs and the

Commission to select Route 894 or any other route not utilizing the G4 Opposition Segments or

territory identified as GCW habitat remembering that the choice of route isn’t the hard part, its

living with what you choose. Choose wisely.

                            II.    SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

       After 5 days of hearing, there was not a single expert, party or landowner that advocated

for any routes utilizing Segments G41, G42, G43, G44, G45 or F8 ("G4 Opposition Segments"),

nor were those segments even mentioned in any cross-examination. They weren't included in any

ofthe focus routes. Furthermore, these 6 segments were included in only 17 ofthe 122 routes (only

13.93%) that were selected and submitted by Casey Petty, PE, PMP to be filed with the CCN




                                                                                    Page 3 of 19
 Application.1 The reason is clear. Routes including these segments underperform in most of the

PURA factor categories listed on the Environmental Assessment.2 At a minimum, they are more

expensive, longer, affect more habitable structures, cross more than double the amount of cultural

resources sites, and come within 1,000 feet of cultural resource sites more than three times than

that of Route 894.3 Staying within at least 500 feet of the centerline, Segment G44 parallels the

Russell Fork ofthe San Gabriel River ("San Gabriel") its entire length and crosses the San Gabriel

numerous times, impetuously fracturing tracts of generational land. Deciding on a route that

includes any of the G4 Opposition Segments makes zero sense and would go against what is

required under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). Making the decision on what

route to choose isn't the hard part, it is living with that choice.

                                           III.   ARGUMENT

              The Underwood Parties are a group of neighbors with property along the G4 Opposition

Segments. They oppose all routes that include the G4 Opposition Segments because of the

significant negative environmental impact and harm to community values in the area, including

the cost, habitable structure count, and the effect on generational land. The ALJs and Commission

should select Route 894 or any other route that avoids the southernmost portion of the study area

and the San Gabriel to avoid these concerns that should be fatal to selection of any route through

that area.
